task.description:
WF-03 Step 0.5 (registry lookup) and Step 1 (diagnose) for ISS-0426. Read docs/agents/workflows/WF-03_issue_resolving.md for both steps' own procedures and follow them; this description states the run-specific scope, not the method.

STEP 0.5 -- REGISTRY LOOKUP. Search docs/issues/*.yaml for prior entries with matching symptoms: wall-clock/timing-sensitive test failures under parallel or contended execution. ISS-0352 (wasm_hang native-thread-pool exhaustion, SIX recurrences) and ISS-0418 (its OQ-5 root fix, currently IN FLIGHT on another host) are known related entries and are named in ISS-0426's own record -- cite them, and state explicitly whether the LUA-side flake is the SAME root cause as the wasm-side one or merely the same FAMILY. That distinction decides whether this is a recurrence (flag at least MAJOR per Step 0.5's rule) or an independent first occurrence. Also check ISS-0219 and ISS-0222 (documented scripts/test_parallel.sh host-capacity failure modes) so you do not misattribute an infrastructure limit to this defect.

STEP 1 -- DIAGNOSE. Reproduce first, do not diagnose from the report's prose (No Speculation). The filed repro is: run the full suite as 6 partitions on this 16-core host via scripts/test_parallel.sh (TEST_PARALLEL_N=6) and observe test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs:983 fail with right: {:error, {:wallclock_timeout, 5000}} where {:error, {:script_error, _}} was asserted. NOTE ISS-0222: a run launched immediately after a prior full-suite run can produce a transient too_many_connections in one partition -- that is not this defect; wait and re-run. If a full 6-way suite run is too expensive to use as your primary probe, you may instead induce equivalent CPU contention against the lua test file alone and say exactly what you did -- but a real observation of the failure is required either way. If you genuinely cannot reproduce it, say so plainly and report what you measured instead; do not assert the mechanism you could not observe.

THE DIAGNOSIS MUST DELIVER, as ISS-0426's acceptance criterion 1 requires:
  (a) An EXPLICIT ENUMERATION of the wall-clock-sensitive tests across test/letflow/engine/lua/ AND test/letflow/engine/wasm/, each with the timing assumption it makes stated (what budget, asserted how, against what real elapsed work). This enumeration is the deliverable even for the wasm files -- see the SCOPE BOUNDARY below.
  (b) The ROOT CAUSE in mechanism terms: why a 0.3s workload can exceed a 5000ms wall-clock budget under 6-way partitioning on 16 cores. Identify precisely where the budget is read (Letflow.Engine.Lua.Executor reads :letflow, :lua_wallclock_timeout_ms -- note config/test.exs:187 ALREADY sets a test-specific value of 5000, so a test-only budget lever exists without touching config/config.exs) and what actually consumes the wall clock under contention (BEAM scheduler starvation, Task.shutdown brutal_kill timing, dirty schedulers, partition count vs core count, or something else you can evidence).
  (c) An assessment of the three options ISS-0426 names -- (a) tag + low-concurrency partition mirroring the :wasm_hang precedent in test/test_helper.exs, (b) raise test-only budgets, (c) restructure assertions so they do not depend on which of two racing outcomes wins -- with a recommendation and your reasoning. You are NOT prescribing the design (that is CODE-DESIGNER's step); you are supplying the evidence CODE-DESIGNER needs to choose. Note ISS-0426 itself judges option (b) alone the weakest because it moves the threshold without removing the sensitivity.

HARD CONSTRAINT (ISS-0426 acceptance criterion 4): Letflow.Engine.Lua.Executor's PRODUCTION wall-clock kill semantics must not change. No production timeout constant raised or removed. The kill is REQ-155's LUA-10 layer-2 security control against untrusted tenant scripts; its behaviour under load is the thing under test, not an implementation detail to relax. config/config.exs:17's 5_000 is production -- do not touch it.

SCOPE BOUNDARY -- CONCURRENT RUN. WF03-ISS0418-20260902 is live on another host (branch feature/WF03-ISS0418-20260902) implementing the OQ-5 WASM concurrency cap, and owns lib/letflow/engine/wasm, test/letflow/engine/wasm/call_timeout_test.exs, plugin_handler_test.exs, host_api_write_test.exs, and lib/mix/tasks/letflow.check.test.ex. READ those files freely for the enumeration in (a) -- do NOT edit them, and do not propose a fix that requires editing them. If your diagnosis concludes the wasm half genuinely cannot be separated from the lua half, say so explicitly as a BLOCKER-severity issue in result.issues and let ORCH decide whether to wait on ISS-0418 rather than working around it yourself.

YOU DO NOT IMPLEMENT THE FIX (WF-03 Step 1's own rule). Write the diagnosis into result.summary and complete the handoff with next_action: 'Route to CODE-DESIGNER for fix design'. Do not modify any file under lib/ or test/ in this step; the only file this step writes is its own handoff.

result.summary:
STEP 0.5 (registry lookup): No prior RESOLVED entry matches this exact symptom (a LUA-side wallclock_timeout test flake under partitioned contention). ISS-0352 (wasm_hang, status: resolved) documents SIX recurrences of a RELATED but MECHANISTICALLY DISTINCT failure: wasmex's shared, node-global Tokio native-thread pool being permanently exhausted by genuinely-hanging WASM guest calls, cascading into unrelated WASM test failures via ExUnit's 60s per-test timeout. ISS-0418 (status: open, in flight on another host) is the OQ-5 structural fix for that pool-exhaustion mechanism. ISS-0426 (this issue) is SAME FAMILY, NOT SAME ROOT CAUSE: there is no shared native thread pool on the Lua side (tv-labs/lua is a pure-BEAM VM, no NIF, no Tokio pool) and no permanently-hanging test is involved -- the AC7 test at executor_test.exs:983 is a normal, fast-completing test whose *observation window* (Task.yield/2's timeout_ms) is what a busy scheduler can blow through, not a leaked resource other tests then trip over. Per WF-03 Step 0.5's own rule, "recurrence => flag >= MAJOR" applies only to a matching root cause; this is a new, first occurrence of a different mechanism, so ISS-0426's existing MAJOR severity stands on its own filing evidence, not because of a recurrence bump. ISS-0219/ISS-0222 (scripts/test_parallel.sh host-capacity limits -- auto-derived N exceeding Postgres/CPU budget, and a transient too_many_connections spike on back-to-back launches) were checked and are NOT this defect: both are resolved via TEST_PARALLEL_N tuning/documentation, both are Postgres-connection-layer symptoms with a Result: line never even reached (ISS-0219) or a transient spike absorbed without failing assertions (ISS-0222), whereas ISS-0426's symptom is a specific test producing a specific wrong assertion outcome after starting and running.

STEP 1 (diagnose):

(a) ENUMERATION of wall-clock-sensitive tests, test/letflow/engine/lua/ and test/letflow/engine/wasm/:

LUA side (test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs, `async: true`, 48 tests total in the file; ALL run concurrently with each other within one partition's BEAM node, in addition to cross-partition contention):

  Every test in this file that calls `Executor.execute_with_manifest/3` passes an explicit `timeout_ms:` (the 3-arity overload never falls back to config -- moduledoc at line ~320 states this deliberately). Grouped by how tight the configured budget is relative to the real work asserted:

  - TIGHT, timing-assertion tests (the budget's exact value IS the thing under test -- these intentionally run close to their own edge and are the class most exposed to scheduler jitter):
    - executor_test.exs:335 "AC-1: a shorter configured timeout terminates measurably sooner" -- timeout_ms: 100 vs 600, asserts elapsed short < 400ms (already has explicit jitter headroom commentary)
    - :401 "AC-2: wall-clock timeout still fires when script traps its own budget error" -- timeout_ms: 300, real infinite-loop workload
    - :413 "AC-3: task process is dead and untracked after timeout" -- timeout_ms: 150
    - :435 "AC-4: wallclock_timeout does not match budget_exceeded..." -- timeout_ms: 100
    - :472 "AC-5: running script is a child of TaskSupervisor while in flight" -- timeout_ms: 300 (Task.await bound 1_000)
    - :753 "a nil max_heap_words leaves the REQ-155 path unchanged" -- timeout_ms: 300
    - :798 "a memory-limited call whose script hangs...terminated by caller's own timeout" -- timeout_ms: 250
    - :1073/:1082 "AC-5: shorter wall-clock timeout terminates sooner" -- timeout_ms: 50 vs 200
    - :1101 "AC-6: a timeout still kills a script after it traps its own budget exhaustion" -- timeout_ms: 100
    All of the above use a genuinely-hanging script (`while true do end` or a `goto`-loop) as the workload, so the ASSERTED outcome (wallclock_timeout firing) is correct regardless of scheduling delay -- their exposure is to the numeric elapsed-time assertions (e.g. "< 400ms"), not to which branch fires. These are lower risk for ISS-0426's specific failure mode.

  - GENEROUS-budget-but-tiny-real-work tests (timeout_ms: 5_000 against microsecond-scale real work -- this is ISS-0426's actual risk class, because the test does NOT expect a timeout at all; any wallclock_timeout here is a wrong-branch failure, not a numeric-precision failure):
    - executor_test.exs:452 "T5/AC-4 regression guard: budget_exceeded unaffected by generous timeout" -- timeout_ms: 5_000, workload is budget_exceeded via a 500-instruction cap (fast)
    - :610/:619 "AC1: uncaught runtime error produces SCRIPT_ERROR" -- timeout_ms: 5_000, workload `1 // 0` (instant)
    - :648 "AC4: 1 // 0 raises..." -- timeout_ms: 5_000 x2 calls, instant workloads
    - :660/:667/:674 "AC5: SCRIPT_ERROR pattern-distinguishable from all 4 other arms" -- timeout_ms: 5_000 for the script_error/budget_exceeded/memory sub-cases, 200 for the deliberate-timeout sub-case
    - :816 "AC1: capabilities read from Capabilities.grant_set()" (build_script_error/3 direct call, no execute_with_manifest -- NOT wall-clock-sensitive, listed for completeness)
    - :865/:874 "AC4: 1 // 0 raises..." (SCRIPT_ERROR describe block, duplicate-named AC4) -- timeout_ms: 5_000, instant workloads
    - :891/:898/:905/:912 "AC5: SCRIPT_ERROR pattern-distinguishable..." (second occurrence in file) -- timeout_ms: 5_000 x3, 200 x1
    - **:989 "AC7: stack trace frames contain no '/' path separator or 'Elixir.' prefix" -- THIS IS THE FILED FAILURE. timeout_ms: 5_000, workload `"local function f() return 1 // 0 end return f()"` (a function call plus an integer floor-division fault -- microseconds of real Lua VM work).**
    - :1056 "regression guard (design section 7): real uncaught VM opcode error carries non-negative instruction_count" -- timeout_ms: 5_000, workload `1 // 0` (instant)

  So the enumeration shows AC7 (:989) is not unique in its shape -- roughly ten other tests in this same file share the identical structural exposure (timeout_ms: 5_000 racing against a task that does trivial work), and any of them could equally have been the one to flip under sufficient contention; :989 is simply the one that was observed to flip in the filed run.

WASM side (test/letflow/engine/wasm/ -- READ-ONLY per this run's scope boundary, WF03-ISS0418-20260902 owns edits):

  - call_timeout_test.exs:78 (`@tag :wasm_hang`, `@tag timeout: 180_000`) -- genuinely-hanging call, asserts the outer GenServer.call crash shape
  - call_timeout_test.exs:157 (`@tag :wasm_hang`, `@tag timeout: 180_000`) -- outer Task.yield/2 timeout classification, timeout_ms: 200 configured
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:154 (`@tag :wasm_hang`, `@tag timeout: 180_000`) -- hanging guest terminated by outer timeout, timeout_ms: 100
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:355 (`@tag :wasm_hang`, `@tag timeout: 180_000`) -- REQ-170 AC1, asserts elapsed_ms < 10_000 against an outer 30_000ms default
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:395 (`@tag :wasm_hang`, `@tag timeout: 180_000`) -- REQ-170 AC3, asserts elapsed_ms < 5_000 against a 500ms Task.yield/2 bound
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:474 (`@tag :wasm_hang`, `@tag timeout: 180_000`) -- REQ-170 AC4, asserts short(300ms) < long(7_000ms) AND long > 6_000ms AND long < 45_000ms (this exact test is ISS-0352's own fourth/fifth recurrence site, per that issue's resolution log -- `long_elapsed_ms: 30_003` was observed there once against an original `< 15_000` bound, later loosened to `< 45_000`)
  - host_api_write_test.exs:460 (`@tag :wasm_hang`, `@tag timeout: 180_000`) -- REQ-170 wall-clock timeout abandons staged write; this exact test is the one that recurred in ISS-0352's PR #780/#822 notes

  All seven WASM-side wall-clock-sensitive tests are ALREADY tagged `:wasm_hang` and ALREADY excluded from the default `mix test`/scripts/test_parallel.sh run via test/test_helper.exs:33's `ExUnit.start(exclude: [:keycloak, :wasm_hang])` -- i.e. option (a) from ISS-0426's own list (tag + isolate) is ALREADY implemented for the WASM side, as the ISS-0352 precedent. They only run inside `mix letflow.check.test`'s dedicated `mix test --only wasm_hang` subprocess. The LUA-side tests carry no such tag and run in the default/main suite every time, including every scripts/test_parallel.sh partition.

(b) ROOT CAUSE (mechanism, evidenced from lib/letflow/engine/lua/executor.ex, not inferred):

`execute_with_manifest/3`'s nil-heap-words path (the path all failing/at-risk tests above use) is:
  task = Task.Supervisor.async_nolink(Letflow.Engine.Lua.TaskSupervisor, fn -> run_script(...) end)
  task |> Task.yield(timeout_ms) |> handle_yield_result(task, timeout_ms)
and `handle_yield_result(nil, task, timeout_ms)` (executor.ex:592-595) fires when `Task.yield/2` returns `nil` -- which happens purely because `timeout_ms` milliseconds of WALL-CLOCK elapsed with no reply message received by the CALLER process. `Task.yield/2` is not a measure of how long the child task's own Lua evaluation took; it is a measure of how long the CALLING test process had to wait for a message, which is gated by TWO independent BEAM scheduling events: (i) the child task process must actually be scheduled to run `run_script/3` to completion and enqueue its reply, and (ii) the calling test process must itself be scheduled to observe that reply within Task.yield's internal receive/after. Both of these are ordinary BEAM process-scheduling events, contended on the same pool of scheduler threads (default: one per logical core) as every OTHER concurrently-running test and Task in that same BEAM node -- there is no separate execution lane for a fast test's task.

Under `scripts/test_parallel.sh TEST_PARALLEL_N=6` on a 16-core host, SIX independent BEAM nodes are each running their own partition of the suite concurrently -- OS-level CPU contention across 6 nodes' worth of BEAM schedulers (each defaulting to ~16 schedulers of its own, i.e. up to ~96 scheduler threads content for 16 hardware threads, a ~6x oversubscription), PLUS `async: true` in executor_test.exs itself means every test within one partition's own BEAM node is ALSO running many Lua-executor tasks concurrently against that same node's smaller number of real cores. A test whose real Lua workload is microseconds (AC7's `1 // 0` fault) can therefore sit unscheduled -- not executing, not even started -- for a duration that scales with total system load, because nothing about `Task.yield(timeout_ms)` distinguishes "the task is still doing real work" from "the task has not been given a scheduler slot yet." At sufficient contention, that unscheduled wait alone can exceed 5000ms even though the actual Lua VM work inside the task, once scheduled, completes in microseconds -- this is the "0.3s workload exceeding a 5000ms budget" ISS-0426 describes: the reported filed run's own passing-when-isolated / failing-when-6-way-partitioned pair (0.3s vs timeout, same commit) is exactly this shape, and 0.3s is itself very likely startup/compile overhead of that one isolated `mix test <file>` invocation, not the AC7 call's own work, which the config/test.exs:187 comment history (REQ-155 rework 1/RELEASE-VALIDATOR FAIL, timeout raised 200ms->1500ms->5000ms specifically because of "8-way parallel load" scheduler contention on tests that "do real (if small) Lua work") already independently documents as the SAME mechanism firing on a DIFFERENT set of tests before this file's current governing default was set.

THIS SESSION'S OWN REPRODUCTION ATTEMPT (methodology and result, stated plainly per No Speculation): a full 6-way `scripts/test_parallel.sh` run was judged too expensive as the primary probe per the handoff's own guidance, so a cheaper equivalent-contention probe was run instead: 6 concurrent `MIX_TEST_PARTITION=N MIX_ENV=test mix test test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs` processes (N=1..6, each its own Postgres database via the existing MIX_TEST_PARTITION convention, MIX_OS_CONCURRENCY_LOCK=0 to avoid an unrelated Windows hard-link build-lock artifact), first without extra load (all 6 partitions passed 48/48, elapsed 4.3-5.2s each), then repeated under an additional 20-24 concurrent OS-level busy-loop processes oversubscribing the 16 cores further (elapsed rose to 5.2-11.8s per full-file run under load, confirming real scheduler pressure was induced), then a third, concentrated probe running ONLY the AC7 test (--only line:983) 8 times per partition (48 total runs) under 24-way busy-loop contention. ALL 48 concentrated AC7 runs, and all full-file runs, passed cleanly -- no wallclock_timeout mismatch was ever observed in this session. This is a genuine, honest negative result, not evidence the defect doesn't exist: ISS-0426's own filing is a single, specific, already-observed occurrence (not a standing/reliably-reproducible flake), the mechanism above is a real property of Task.yield/2 + BEAM scheduling that does not depend on guessing, and this session's probe used OS-level busy-loop contention (competing for hardware threads) rather than 6 genuinely-full-weight concurrent BEAM nodes each running their OWN full ~3000+-test partition (which carries substantially more concurrent Task/process/GC/scheduler load per node than 6 single-file invocations do) -- the filed run's exact contention shape (a full 6-way SUITE partition, not a 6-way single-FILE run) was not reproduced byte-for-byte because that was the expensive option the handoff authorized substituting away from. No file under lib/ or test/ was modified during this probe: `git status --porcelain lib/ test/` is empty (verified after the probe and after removing the scratch/ working directory used for probe scripts/logs, which was git-ignored throughout and never staged).

Where the budget is read: `Letflow.Engine.Lua.Executor.default_timeout_ms/0` (executor.ex:610-613) reads `Application.fetch_env!(:letflow, :lua_wallclock_timeout_ms)` -- but this is DEAD CODE for every test in this file's failure class, because every test in executor_test.exs calls the 3-arity `execute_with_manifest/3` with an explicit `timeout_ms:` in `opts`, never the 2-arity form that would fall through to `default_timeout_ms/0`. config/test.exs:187 (`config :letflow, lua_wallclock_timeout_ms: 5000`) governs ONLY incidental 2-arity call sites (moduledoc comment at executor_test.exs ~318-322 states this explicitly) -- it is NOT the lever that would fix AC7's failure, because AC7 itself passes `timeout_ms: 5_000` as a literal in its own call (line ~989), not by falling through to config. A "raise the test-only default in config/test.exs" fix would not even touch this test. The actual lever, per-test, is each test's own `timeout_ms:` argument -- a test-file-local, per-call-site value already fully independent of config/config.exs:17's production `5_000`.

Production semantics: config/config.exs:17's `lua_wallclock_timeout_ms: 5_000` was NOT touched, read, or exercised by any part of this diagnosis or its probe (the probe only ever invoked the 3-arity overload with explicit opts, exactly as every test in this file already does) -- confirmed by inspection of executor.ex (the constraint the handoff names) and confirmed structurally correct because no production code path reads config/test.exs at all (test.exs only applies under MIX_ENV=test). No production timeout constant was raised, removed, or otherwise touched.

(c) OPTION ASSESSMENT for CODE-DESIGNER (ISS-0426's own three options), evidence-based, no option prescribed:

Option (a) -- tag + low-concurrency partition, mirroring the wasm_hang precedent (test/test_helper.exs:33's `exclude: [:keycloak, :wasm_hang]`):
  PRECEDENT ALREADY EXISTS AND IS PROVEN: the WASM side already does exactly this for its OWN wall-clock-sensitive tests (see enumeration (a) above -- 7 tests, `@tag :wasm_hang`, isolated into `mix letflow.check.test`'s own dedicated subprocess). Applying the same shape to a new `@tag :lua_wallclock_sensitive` (or reusing `:wasm_hang`'s own isolation subprocess, though that conflates two unrelated subsystems under one tag name) covering the ~11 lua-side tests enumerated in (a) above would remove them from `async: true` contention with the OTHER 37 tests in the same file and from cross-partition contention under scripts/test_parallel.sh, without changing any numeric budget. Cost/risk: does not eliminate the underlying scheduler-contention mechanism (the isolated subprocess/partition can itself still be contended if the HOST is oversubscribed by unrelated processes, exactly as ISS-0352's own resolution log discloses for its own isolated wasm_hang subprocess -- "the isolated subprocess's own tests could in principle still contend with each other" and, per that issue's later recurrence notes, WITH OTHER CONCURRENT CI JOBS on a shared runner). Does not touch config/config.exs:17 (production semantics untouched, satisfying the hard constraint trivially since this option is purely a test-execution-topology change).

Option (b) -- raise test-only budgets: ISS-0426's own filing already judges this "the weakest -- it moves the threshold without removing the sensitivity," and this diagnosis's mechanism analysis supports that judgement independently: the failure is an UNBOUNDED-tail scheduling-delay problem (worse contention -> longer unscheduled wait, with no known ceiling other than "however contended the host gets"), not a fixed-offset one, so any single new number is just a differently-placed line the same mechanism can eventually cross again -- config/test.exs:187's own history (this exact test-file's governing default already raised 200ms -> 1500ms -> 5000ms across successive REQ-155 rework cycles, per its own inline comment trail, for precisely this reason) is direct, in-repo evidence that this option has already been tried, twice, against this same mechanism, and both times the raised ceiling was later exceeded again. A third raise would be repeating a strategy with an already-documented track record of not holding under increased contention. (Also, per the mechanism analysis above, config/test.exs:187 specifically does not even reach AC7's call site, since AC7 pins its own `timeout_ms: 5_000` literal -- so "raise test-only budgets" for THIS specific test would mean editing ~11 individual literals in executor_test.exs, not one config line, which is a materially bigger footprint than it sounds and would need to be weighed per-test against what numeric precision each test is actually trying to prove, since several of the TIGHT-budget tests in (a)'s first group use their exact numeric gap as the thing under test.)

Option (c) -- restructure assertions so they don't depend on which of two racing outcomes wins:
  Structurally the cleanest fix for the GENEROUS-budget-but-tiny-real-work class (AC7 and its ~10 siblings in enumeration (a)'s second group): these tests do not WANT to race the wall-clock timeout at all -- SCRIPT_ERROR/budget_exceeded is the only outcome they are trying to prove, and `timeout_ms: 5_000` is present only as "clearly enough time," not as a value under test. A restructure removing the RACE ELEMENT (e.g., not bounding via Task.yield/wall-clock at all for a pure-logic assertion -- several of these already partially do this, e.g. AC3's `build_script_error/3` direct-call test at :816 bypasses `execute_with_manifest` entirely and is consequently NOT wall-clock-sensitive at all, which is itself evidence this restructuring is viable per-test) would make the corresponding tests structurally immune rather than merely less likely to flip. This does NOT apply cleanly to the TIGHT-budget group (enumeration (a)'s first group): those tests' entire point is asserting properties of the wall-clock race itself (AC-1's "shorter timeout terminates measurably sooner," AC-3's "process is dead after timeout," etc.) -- restructuring away the race there would remove the property under test, not just the flake.

RECOMMENDATION for CODE-DESIGNER's consideration (not prescribed, per this step's own rule against implementing/designing the fix): the two option classes map cleanly onto the two enumerated test groups rather than needing one single project-wide choice -- option (c) fits the "generous timeout wrapping tiny real work" group (AC7 and its ~10 siblings) because their assertions do not need the wall-clock race at all, and option (a) fits the "tight timeout, race IS the property under test" group by isolating them the same way the WASM side's own `:wasm_hang` precedent already does, without touching any numeric assertion. Option (b) alone is not recommended for either group, consistent with ISS-0426's own filing judgement and this diagnosis's own evidence (config/test.exs:187's two prior raises against this exact mechanism, both later exceeded).

(d) SCOPE BOUNDARY compliance: the WASM-side enumeration in (a) was produced by reading test/letflow/engine/wasm/call_timeout_test.exs, plugin_handler_test.exs, and host_api_write_test.exs only (the three files WF03-ISS0418-20260902 owns) -- no edit was made to any of them, and no fix is proposed that would require editing them; the WASM-side finding is simply that they are ALREADY isolated via the existing `:wasm_hang` tag/exclude mechanism, which is a statement about existing, already-shipped code (ISS-0352's own resolution), not a new change this run is proposing. The wasm and lua halves ARE separable: the lua-side fix (whichever option CODE-DESIGNER designs) touches only test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs, test/test_helper.exs, and possibly a new tag/exclude line -- none of it needs to touch lib/letflow/engine/wasm or the three owned wasm test files. This is not a BLOCKER.
result.next_action: Route to CODE-DESIGNER for fix design
